about: Physics blocks whose maths is a formula (ND3b): each keeps its id, ports and results, and its maths is the Equation below, with a name that says what happens.

params.description: air pressure at the boundary over the wind's ram pressure (stand-in for the ionosphere's share)

references: Brace, L. H. and Kliore, A. J. 1991, The structure of the Venus ionosphere, Space Sci. Rev. 55, 81: the ionopause sits where the ionosphere's pressure balances the solar wind's, a few hundred km up on Venus. doi:10.1007/BF00177136
Luhmann, J. G. and Cravens, T. E. 1991, Magnetic fields in the ionosphere of Venus, Space Sci. Rev. 55, 201: induced magnetospheres of unmagnetised bodies with air. doi:10.1007/BF00177137

equation.name: Height where a world's air holds off the wind
equation.formula:
P0 = max(P, 0)
ram = max(rho, 0) * v * v
h = if P0 <= 0 or ram <= 0 then 0 else max(H * ln(P0 / (k * ram)), 0)

H.name: height over which the pressure falls to a third

k.name: air pressure at the boundary over the wind's push

h.name: height where the air holds the wind off

source.text: Brace, L. H. and Kliore, A. J. 1991, Space Sci. Rev. 55, 81

explain.curious: A world with air but no magnetic field still holds the wind off: the wind lights up the top of its air and pushes against that. Venus and Mars do this a few hundred kilometres up.
explain.science: The wind's ram pressure meets the upper atmosphere's pressure in an isothermal column. A stand-in for the ionospheric pressure balance, which needs the ionosphere's own profile.

params.description: north-south field in the wind, nT (southward negative)

references: Shue, J.-H. et al. 1998, Magnetopause location under extreme solar wind conditions, J. Geophys. Res. 103, 17691: r = r₀ (2 / (1 + cos θ))^α, α = (0.58 − 0.007 B_z)(1 + 0.024 ln P_dyn), B_z in nT, P_dyn in nPa. doi:10.1029/98JA01103

equation.name: How the magnetic boundary flares behind a world
equation.formula:
ram = max(rho, 0) * v * v
bt = bz * nT
p = max(ram * per_nPa, floor)
alpha = (a0 - a1 * bt * per_nT) * (1 + a2 * ln(p))

bz.name: north-south field in the wind, nT

alpha.name: how much the boundary flares behind the world

source.text: Shue, J.-H. et al. 1998, J. Geophys. Res. 103, 17691

explain.curious: The bubble is blunt at the nose and flares out behind into a long tail; a stronger wind or a southward field opens it wider.
explain.science: Shue's empirical boundary: distance r₀ at the nose, flaring with angle from the nose by the exponent α.

references: Kivelson, M. G. et al. 1998, Ganymede's magnetosphere: magnetometer overview, J. Geophys. Res. 103, 19963: a moon's own field stands off its host's field and plasma about two moon radii out. doi:10.1029/98JE00227

equation.name: Where a moon's own field holds off its host's
equation.formula:
m0 = max(M, 0)
b = max(B, 0)
bn = sqrt(b * b + 2 * mu0 * max(max(p, 0), 0))
R = if m0 <= 0 or bn <= 0 then 0 else cbrt(mu0 * m0 / (2 * pi * bn))

M.name: strength of the moon's magnet (dipole moment)

B.name: host's field where the moon orbits

p.name: plasma pressure where the moon orbits

R.name: where the moon's field holds the host's off

source.text: Kivelson, M. G. et al. 1998, J. Geophys. Res. 103, 19963

explain.curious: A moon with its own field inside a planet's bubble makes a bubble within a bubble. Ganymede's reaches about two of its own widths out against Jupiter's field.
explain.science: Inside a host's bubble the pressure outside is the host's field and plasma, not the star's wind. The moon's compressed dipole balances them.

references: Zimmer, C., Khurana, K. K. and Kivelson, M. G. 2000, Subsurface oceans on Europa and Callisto: constraints from Galileo magnetometer observations, Icarus 147, 329: a conducting shell answers a changing field with a dipole of relative strength A. doi:10.1006/icar.2000.6456

Kivelson, M. G. et al. 2000, Galileo magnetometer measurements: a stronger case for a subsurface ocean at Europa, Science 289, 1340: induced response close to that of a perfect conductor (A about 0.97). doi:10.1126/science.289.5483.1340
atoms.shown: A = κ / √(1 + κ²),  κ = μ₀ σ ω r min(h, δ) / 3,  δ = √(2 / μ₀σω)

equation.name: How strongly a buried ocean answers a changing field
equation.formula:
s = max(sigma, 0)
d = max(h, 0)
omega = 2 * pi / T
hs = min(d, sqrt(2 / (mu0 * s * omega)))
k = mu0 * s * omega * r * hs / 3
A = if s <= 0 or d <= 0 or T <= 0 then 0 else k / sqrt(1 + k * k)

A.name: share of the change the layer answers back

source.text: Zimmer, C., Khurana, K. K. and Kivelson, M. G. 2000, Icarus 147, 329

explain.curious: A salty ocean under ice is a conductor. As a moon swings through its planet's tilted field, the ocean answers with a field of its own, and a magnetometer flying past can find the hidden sea.
explain.science: A thin conducting shell in a field changing at angular frequency ω answers with a dipole of relative strength κ/√(1+κ²), κ = μ₀σωrh/3; a shell thicker than the skin depth acts as one skin depth thick.
